claims.text: TGA combined with in situ high-temperature XRD can effectively monitor high-temperature oxidation behaviour and phase stability in metal alloys.
The initial alloy is homogeneous and has a clean surface without significant pre-existing oxide layers.
The alloy is heated in a controlled oxidizing environment such as air or oxygen.
An operating range of 800–1200°C is above the oxidation onset for the alloy.
High-temperature oxidation causes surface oxide scales to form and grow.
The surface oxide scales influence the phase stability of the underlying alloy.
Oxygen interaction with the alloy at high temperature forms oxide layers.
Oxide-layer formation produces a measurable sample-weight gain detectable by TGA.
Concurrent phase transformations can be tracked through the appearance and evolution of distinct XRD peaks.
Sample-mass increase will correlate with the formation of oxide phases.
In situ XRD will show emerging or transforming crystal structures associated with oxide scales and altered alloy phases.
The combined method may have limited ability to resolve very subtle phase transitions.
XRD may have difficulty distinguishing oxides with similar diffraction patterns.
Extreme high-temperature conditions may impair instrument stability.
The sensitivity and coupling efficiency of simultaneous TGA and in situ XRD for oxidation-induced phase changes have not been fully quantified in this context.
